- **Speedup:** Searches that would take much longer manually were completed in <1 day; no defensible numerical speedup versus grid or OFAT was explicitly reported (pqac-00000003).

---

### 3. Helmholtz Institute Münster / Stein Robotic HTE System — Non-Aqueous, N₂ Atmosphere (Rahmanian et al., 2023)

A high-throughput experimentation system for non-aqueous battery electrolyte formulation with automated conductivity measurement via EIS (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046).

- **DOI:** 10.1038/s41597-023-01936-3 (Scientific Data, 2023); related one-shot active-learning study: 10.1002/batt.202200228 (Rahmanian et al., 2022); related ML-aided optimization: 10.1039/d3ta06249j (Yan et al., 2024)
- **What was dosed:** Both liquids and solids — gravimetric dosing of EC, PC, EMC (liquids), and LiPF₆ (solid salt) into aluminium or polymer vials with automated closure, mixing, heating, and electrode immersion (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046).
- **Conductivity measurement:** Automated electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) after thermal equilibration from −30 to 60 °C in 10 °C steps; 40 mV AC excitation over 20 kHz–50 Hz; MADAP software performed Arrhenius analysis (pqac-00000046).
- **Compositions per campaign:** Up to 96 formulations in 8 hours; dataset comprises 504 formulation JSON files and 5,035 individual experiments/measurements; the Flores et al. symbolic-regression study used 3,626 individual measurements aggregated into 859 data points (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000048).
- **Optimizer:** The 2023 dataset paper did not incorporate a closed-loop optimizer (MADAP is downstream analysis software). The related 2022 publication used one-shot active learning for globally optimal conductivity. The system operated in a controlled N₂ atmosphere (pqac-00000046).
- **Speedup:** 96 formulations per 8 hours represents high throughput; no explicit grid/OFAT speedup was reported in the available evidence.

---

### 4. Self-Driving CO₂ Electrolyser — Aqueous (Deng et al., 2026)

This platform demonstrates closed-loop electrolyte optimization but with ethylene selectivity (not conductivity) as the feedback signal (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000030).

- **DOI:** Not yet established in the available record (2026 manuscript).
- **What was dosed:** Liquids only — aqueous Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, and Cs⁺ stocks dispensed by precision syringe pumps through a passive four-way mixing junction; DI-water flushing between formulations; no powder dosing.
- **Measurement:** Inline DGS2 C₂H₄ gas sensor (not ionic conductivity); GC validation.
- **Compositions per campaign:** 45 unique compositions per current-density condition, initialized from 22 training points; three current densities studied; quaternary design space >170,000 compositions at 1% resolution (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025).
- **Optimizer:** TuRBO (trust-region Bayesian optimization) with Gaussian-process surrogate (pqac-00000025).
- **Speedup:** Each formulation evaluated in <10 min; blended compositions improved relative C₂H₄ selectivity by 5–10% over best single-cation systems; no explicit grid/OFAT sample reduction reported.

---

### 5. Additional Related Platforms (Not Strict Conductivity-Closed-Loop)

**ODACell (Yik et al., 2023; DOI: 10.1039/D3DD00058C):** An affordable, modular robotic system for automated electrolyte formulation, coin-cell assembly, and galvanostatic cycling using Opentrons OT-2 liquid handling and Dobot robotic arms. Demonstrated with aqueous LiClO₄/DMSO model electrolytes. Measures cycling performance, not standalone ionic conductivity. No closed-loop optimizer; 83 cells assembled in six batches with ~2% capacity RSD (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034).

**Electrolab (Oh et al., 2023; DOI: 10.1016/j.device.2023.100103):** An open-source, modular platform for automated characterization of redox-active electrolytes. Uses an XYZ gantry robot, multiplexed microelectrode arrays, and Python/Arduino control. Demonstrated voltammetric screening (200 voltammograms in 2 hours) and solution titration, not bulk ionic conductivity. Bayesian optimization proposed for future work; glovebox-compatible version planned (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000020).

**SALSA (Zhang et al., 2026; DOI: 10.1039/D5DD00516G):** A ~US$100 modular add-on to the Clio/ElyteOS platform for automated salt solubility assessment. Uses a 3D-printed Archimedes-screw solid doser and computer-vision dissolution detection. Demonstrated with NaFSI in ACN, DME, and EMC. Measures solubility, not conductivity (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043).

**Auto-MISCHBARES (Rahmanian et al., 2024; DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-rb9j7):** An autonomous millimetre-scale battery research system using a Hamilton Microlab 600 syringe and HELAO active-learning software. Full details were not obtainable, and ionic-conductivity measurement was not established in the available evidence (pqac-00000041).

**PNNL Robotic Solubility Platform (Noh et al., 2024; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-47070-5):** A closed-loop platform for discovering electrolyte solvents for non-aqueous redox-flow batteries. Dosed both solid redox-active molecules and organic solvents; measured solubility by quantitative NMR, not conductivity. Used Bayesian optimization with GP regression; screened <10% of >2,000 candidates, achieving >90% sample reduction and >13× throughput advantage (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000029).

---

### Key Observations

1. **True closed-loop conductivity optimization** has been demonstrated by very few platforms. The clearest example is **Clio/Dragonfly** (Dave et al., 2022), which is the only platform in the retrieved literature that combines automated liquid dosing, in-line ionic conductivity measurement, and Bayesian-optimization-driven next-experiment selection in a single closed loop for battery electrolyte formulation (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039).

2. **Aqueous vs. non-aqueous distinction:** The CMU Autonomous Test Stand (Whitacre et al., 2019) operated with aqueous electrolytes at ambient conditions (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005). Clio (Dave et al., 2022) operated with non-aqueous carbonate electrolytes inside a dry-argon glovebox (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000047). The Helmholtz HTE system operated under N₂ atmosphere with non-aqueous carbonates (pqac-00000046).

3. **Platforms named in the query but not matching the specific scope:** A-Lab is a solid-state inorganic synthesis robot (not liquid electrolyte formulation); ChemOS is orchestration software used by MEDUSA for metal-ligand complexes (not electrolyte conductivity); Otto Chemistry is an organic synthesis robot; none of these were found to have demonstrated liquid electrolyte formulation with conductivity-closed-loop optimization in the retrieved literature (pqac-00000021).

4. **Chemspeed-based electrolyte platforms:** Although the Helmholtz/Münster group's system handles both liquid and solid dosing under inert atmosphere—capabilities consistent with Chemspeed hardware—the retrieved papers do not explicitly identify the robot manufacturer. The associated Krishnamoorthy et al. (2022; DOI: 10.1002/cmtd.202200008) data-driven analysis of high-throughput conductivity experiments was referenced but the full paper was not obtainable.

5. **Sample-count reductions:** The most quantitative claim is from Clio/Dragonfly: ~96% fewer samples versus exhaustive grid search and ~6× time acceleration versus random search (pqac-00000039). The PNNL solubility platform (Noh et al., 2024) reported >90% sample reduction for solubility screening (pqac-00000029).

The study performed 40 experimental evaluations and lists seven named electrolyte blends (A–G), including a priori baseline blend G. contexts.context: The excerpt documents the Whitacre et al. autonomous electrochemical test stand, a relevant example of a closed-loop platform for liquid-electrolyte formulation and characterization. It uses calibrated positive-displacement pumps to dose liquid ingredients, a rotary-valve architecture for selecting constituents, a 3-way valve for routing fluid to waste or the mixing vessel, and a vortex-mixed 10 mL stainless-steel vessel. A second metering pump transfers the mixed electrolyte through flow-through measurement devices. Ionic conductivity and pH are measured using a conductivity probe and micro-pH probe, while a flow-through three-electrode electrochemical cell and potentiostat measure voltage stability behavior. LabVIEW controls the pumps, valves, measurements, and data collection; a Python API issues experiment commands, and machine-learning software orders experiments using electrolyte models as statistical priors. The system includes flushing/cleaning through waste routing and supports formulations containing multiple distinct liquid constituents. Its electrochemical screening protocol applies stepped cathodic and anodic currents and summarizes voltage stability using extrapolated tangent lines. However, this excerpt does not provide information about the other platforms named in the question—Electrolab, AMPERE, Chemspeed systems, A-Lab, Otto Chemistry, ChemOS, or other independent high-throughput conductivity platforms—so it cannot substantiate comparisons or a broader platform inventory.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents one autonomous liquid-electrolyte platform: a fully automated, computer-controlled test stand developed at Carnegie Mellon University. It can combine up to 10 liquid precursors—solvated salt solutions or pure solvents—using a rotary stream-selector valve and precision pump, then automatically characterize the resulting electrolyte. The demonstrated measurements include pH, ionic conductivity, and electrochemical voltage-stability window. Its conductivity standard error was 0.5 mS/cm, and its voltage-window measurement standard error was 0.02 V. The system rapidly explored two-dimensional co-solvated aqueous electrolyte compositions containing sodium or lithium cations and sulfate or nitrate anions; searches that would take much longer manually were completed in less than a day. The authors describe the intended closed-loop architecture as integration with machine-learning software that uses collected data and computational models to select subsequent experiments according to user-defined objectives. However, this paper primarily reports the experimental hardware and autonomous data-acquisition stand; the machine-learning integration was identified as future work. The platform is also described as compatible with organic solvent solutions and potentially applicable to lithium-ion battery electrolytes. It reports an electrolyte titration experiment used to identify optimal solution conditions for redox polymer performance, making Electrolab directly relevant to liquid-electrolyte formulation and closed-loop optimization. contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide details about the Noh et al. integrated high-throughput robotic platform, including what it dosed, its measurement method, number of compositions, optimizer, or speedup. For Deng et al.’s self-driving CO2 electrolyser (SDE), the target was optimization of aqueous alkali-electrolyte blends containing Li+, Na+, K+, and Cs+ for ethylene production. The nominal design space contains more than 170,000 quaternary compositions at 1% composition resolution, although the reported closed-loop campaign used 45 TuRBO iterations per current-density condition, beginning with 22 training data points. The system dosed electrolyte blends automatically into a membrane-electrode assembly (MEA): syringe pumps dispensed the individual electrolytes, a four-way junction passively mixed them, and a reservoir/peristaltic pump delivered the mixture to the cell. Product gas was sampled inline, diluted 65-fold with air, and analyzed using a DGS2 commercial C2H4 sensor; GC-vial samples provided calibration and served as a liquid trap. TuRBO used Gaussian-process surrogate modeling and trust regions to balance exploration and exploitation. The platform included automated water flushing of the reservoir and MEA to remove residual cations between formulations, enabling continuous screening without cell disassembly. It evaluated each new formulation in under 10 minutes, with less than 5% deviation from GC validation. No explicit numerical speedup over the Noh platform is stated in the excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Noh et al.’s closed-loop platform for discovering electrolyte solvents for nonaqueous redox-flow batteries. The model redox-active molecule (ROM) dosed was 2,1,3-benzothiadiazole (BTZ), while the robotic system dispensed both BTZ powder and organic solvents. Prepared saturated solutions were stabilized for 8 hours at a fixed temperature to reach thermodynamic equilibrium, automatically sampled into NMR tubes, and analyzed by quantitative NMR to determine molar solubility. The candidate space comprised 22 single solvents and 2,079 binary solvent compositions, generated by pairing the 22 solvents at nine volume fractions. The reported throughput was 42 solubility measurements in approximately 27 hours, or about 39 minutes per sample, and the excerpt indicates this represented more than a 13-fold advantage in the relevant comparison, although the sentence is truncated. Planned improvements included camera-based monitoring, position calibration for more reliable component placement, and closed-system electrolyte storage to reduce ambient exposure. contexts.context: The excerpt provides details only on Yik et al.’s ODACell platform; it does not describe Fisker-Bødker’s AMPERE-2, SALSA, or Chemspeed-based electrolyte platforms with conductivity measurement. ODACell was developed to automate electrolyte formulation, dispensing, coin-cell assembly, and electrochemical testing for high-throughput lithium-ion battery research. The authors demonstrated ambient-atmosphere assembly of LiFePO4‖Li4Ti5O12 full cells using a dimethyl-sulfoxide-based model electrolyte and investigated the effect of water contamination, including electrolytes containing 2 vol% and 4 vol% added water. The system is designed to reduce manual errors and cell-to-cell variation while enabling large batches of standard-format coin cells. Its reproducibility testing produced a conservative 5% fail rate, and the relative standard deviation of discharge capacity after 10 cycles was 2% for the studied system. contexts.context: The excerpt describes two automated electrolyte platforms that combine liquid handling, conductivity measurement, and software control. The aqueous-electrolyte system uses a robotic test stand to mix feeder solutions and measure pH, ionic conductivity, and electrochemical properties in a symmetric platinum-electrode cell. Its control software exchanges experiment requests, measurements, and metadata through HTTP with a Python API; Dragonfly Bayesian optimization software uses that API to request experiments and receive feedback, establishing a closed-loop autonomous optimization workflow. The non-aqueous platform, called “Clio,” uses programmatic pumps, a 24-port valve, a three-way valve, a common vessel with sonication for mixing, and a waste vessel to formulate and transfer liquid samples. contexts.context: Whitacre et al. describe an autonomous, computer-controlled platform for liquid electrolyte formulation and electrochemical characterization. The system can combine up to 10 liquid precursors, including solvated salt solutions or pure solvents, using a 10-port rotary selector valve and a precision positive-displacement pump. It was designed to make arbitrary-composition electrolytes, rapidly measure multiple properties, and publish results to a shared database. Demonstrated measurements included pH, ionic conductivity, and electrochemical voltage stability window; the reported conductivity standard error was 0.5 mS/cm, and voltage-window error was 0.02 V. In tests of two-dimensional aqueous sulfate/nitrate co-solvent or co-salt spaces, the platform completed searches in less than a day. The authors describe the system as compatible with organic solvents and intended future application to lithium-ion battery electrolytes. Its planned integration with machine-learning software would use measured data and computational models to select subsequent experiments according to user-defined objectives, constituting a prospective closed-loop optimization workflow. contexts.context: The excerpt describes Clio, a custom robotic platform for automated formulation and characterization of nonaqueous liquid battery electrolytes. Clio doses electrolyte compositions from pre-made feeder solutions, with samples created by mixing up to 19 feeder solutions. It measures ionic conductivity along with viscosity, density, and UV-vis spectra; experiments are run in triplicate, and the reported repeatability for conductivity is a mean absolute difference of ±1.3% across tested electrolytes. The system rinses between compositions, can retain samples for pouch-cell testing, and is controlled through HTTP: formulations are submitted as JSON and measurement results are returned electronically. Clio is integrated with Dragonfly, an open-source Bayesian-optimization experiment planner, creating a closed-loop liquid-dosing/conductivity optimization workflow. The demonstrated design space was an EC-DMC-EMC ternary solvent system with LiPF6 as the single salt, optimizing solvent mass fraction and salt molality. The platform identified six fast-charging electrolytes in 42 experiments over two workdays, compared with exhaustive evaluation of 1,000 candidates. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies two liquid-electrolyte automation platforms. First, an autonomous aqueous-electrolyte system uses a robotic test stand to mix feeder solutions and measure pH, ionic conductivity, and electrochemical properties in a symmetric platinum-electrode cell. Its control software communicates through an HTTP/Python API, while Dragonfly Bayesian optimization requests experiments and receives measurements and metadata in a closed loop. Second, “Clio” is an automated non-aqueous electrolyte platform. It uses programmable pumps, a 24-port valve, and a three-way valve to dose and transfer liquid samples from feeder solutions, with sonication-based mixing. Samples are characterized using a dual platinum-wire conductivity chamber, potentiostat, mass balance, and viscometer, under LabVIEW orchestration and glovebox argon handling. The excerpt does not state whether Clio itself was coupled to Bayesian optimization or active learning, nor does it provide speedup, experiment-count, or sample-count reduction figures for either platform. Thus, it supports identification of the aqueous Dragonfly-coupled system and Clio as conductivity-measuring liquid-electrolyte platforms, but not quantitative efficiency comparisons.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports one directly relevant closed-loop platform: Clio, a custom robotic liquid-electrolyte experimentation system coupled to Dragonfly, an open-source Bayesian-optimization experiment planner. Clio doses electrolyte formulations from pre-made feeder solutions and measures ionic conductivity along with viscosity, UV-vis spectrum, and density. The demonstrated design space was a ternary solvent system—ethylene carbonate (EC), ethyl-methyl carbonate (EMC), and dimethyl carbonate (DMC)—with LiPF6 as the single salt; optimization varied solvent mass fraction and salt molality. The system identified six fast-charging electrolytes in two work-days using 42 experiments. The authors compare this with exhaustive evaluation of 1,000 candidates, estimated at 60 days, implying approximately a 30-fold reduction in elapsed experimental time and a 95.8% reduction in tested samples relative to exhaustive search. The excerpt also states that conductivity measurements were run in triplicate and that repeated conductivity measurements differed by an average absolute amount of ±1.3%. Clio communicates through HTTP using JSON, allowing integration with experiment planners. No other autonomous liquid-electrolyte platform is described in the provided pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Clio, a custom robotic, closed-loop electrolyte experimentation platform, rather than identifying the system used specifically by Rahmanian, Stein, Winter, and Cekic-Laskovic. Clio combines automated dosing, mixing, conductivity measurement, experiment management, and machine-learning/Bayesian experiment planning. The system was operated in a dry-argon glovebox, with moisture maintained below 10 ppm. Conductivity was measured using impedance spectroscopy in a PTFE cell with symmetric platinum electrodes; measurements were collected at five frequencies between 14 kHz and 800 kHz, and the resistance at the frequency with the smallest phase difference was used to calculate specific conductivity. The excerpt does not state that Clio was Chemspeed-based; it instead names custom components, including a Fluid Metering stepper-motor pump, a programmable Valco valve set, and a Palmsens4 impedance instrument. The investigated carbonate solvents included ethylene carbonate (EC), dimethyl carbonate (DMC), ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), and diethyl carbonate (DEC), with LiPF6 as the salt. It reports 120 triplicate samples for repeatability testing, but does not give the total number of formulations tested in the optimization. The work used a Bayesian, machine-learning-guided closed-loop optimizer and reports approximately a threefold overall speed-up.

Question: State of the art: which self-driving laboratories / autonomous experimentation platforms have been demonstrated for LIQUID ELECTROLYTE FORMULATION, where an automated liquid-dosing system mixes multi-component solutions and IONIC CONDUCTIVITY is measured in a closed loop to select the next composition? Name the specific platforms (e.g. Clio/Dragonfly, Otto Chemistry, AMANDA/Autonomous Energy Materials Discovery, ChemOS, Chemspeed-based electrolyte platforms, A-Lab, Argonne/NREL electrolyte robots) with DOIs and publication years. For each: what was dosed (liquid only, or powders/salts too), how conductivity was measured (dip probe, flow cell, four-electrode, impedance/potentiostat), how many compositions per campaign, what optimizer was used, and what the reported speedup or sample-count reduction versus grid/one-factor-at-a-time was. Distinguish clearly between aqueous and non-aqueous (glovebox) systems.

## Self-Driving Laboratories for Liquid Electrolyte Formulation with Ionic Conductivity Feedback: State of the Art

### Overview

A systematic search of the literature reveals that only a small number of platforms have demonstrated the full closed-loop cycle of automated liquid-dosing → multi-component electrolyte mixing → ionic conductivity measurement → optimizer-guided next-composition selection. Several additional platforms automate electrolyte formulation and electrochemical characterization but optimize a different target (solubility, cell cycling, or product selectivity) rather than conductivity. The following sections describe each platform, distinguishing those with genuine closed-loop conductivity optimization from those with related but distinct feedback loops.

The table below provides a comprehensive comparison of all identified platforms.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Clio + Dragonfly** | Dave et al. (2022), [10.1038/s41467-022-32938-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-32938-1) | **Non-aqueous; strict match:** formulation, conductivity measurement, and next-composition selection were closed-loop | Dry-Ar glovebox; H₂O below 10 ppm | **Liquids only during campaigns:** premade feeder solutions of LiPF₆ in EC, DMC, and EMC; salt molality and ternary solvent fractions varied; up to 19 feeds; no powder dosing | Flow-through custom PTFE chamber with symmetric Pt electrodes and PalmSens4 impedance analyzer; five frequencies from 14 to 800 kHz; resistance selected at minimum phase angle; calibrated cell constant; triplicate runs | **42 total experiments in two workdays**; conductivity optimum found within about 15 experiments; 120 separate samples in repeatability study | **Dragonfly Bayesian optimization:** Gaussian-process surrogate; Thompson sampling, expected improvement, top-two EI, and UCB acquisitions, plus random exploration | **6× acceleration over random search on the same robot**; about 3× workflow efficiency versus an 8-hour-per-day human workflow; 42 versus nominally 1,000 exhaustive candidates means 95.8% fewer samples, although that grid comparison is extrapolated (dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 1-7, dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 7-12, dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 16-21, dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 12-16) |

*Table: Comparison of strict conductivity-feedback self-driving laboratories and closely related electrolyte-automation systems. It distinguishes genuine closed-loop ionic-conductivity demonstrations from platforms optimizing solubility, cycling performance, or product selectivity.*

---

### 1. Clio / Dragonfly — Non-Aqueous, Glovebox (Dave et al., 2022)

**The closest match to the user's query.** Clio is a custom-built robotic platform operating inside a dry-argon glovebox (H₂O < 10 ppm) that autonomously formulates non-aqueous Li-ion battery electrolytes and measures ionic conductivity in a closed loop (dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 1-7, dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 16-21).

- **DOI:** 10.1038/s41467-022-32938-1 (Nature Communications, 2022)
- **What was dosed:** Liquids only — premade feeder solutions of LiPF₆ dissolved in ethylene carbonate (EC), dimethyl carbonate (DMC), ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), and diethyl carbonate (DEC); up to 19 feeder solutions; salt molality (0–2 mol/kg) and ternary solvent mass fractions were varied. No dry-powder dosing during campaigns (dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 7-12, dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 21-31).
- **Conductivity measurement:** Custom PTFE flow-through cell with symmetric platinum electrodes connected to a PalmSens4 potentiostat/impedance analyzer; impedance spectroscopy at five frequencies (14–800 kHz); resistance determined at the frequency with the smallest phase angle; cell constant calibrated with acetonitrile standard; triplicate measurements with ±1.3% mean absolute percentage error (dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 16-21).
- **Compositions per campaign:** 42 total experiments over two work-days; conductivity optimum (~13.7 mS/cm for EC:DMC 40:60 with 0.9 m LiPF₆ at 26–28 °C) was identified within ~15 experiments; a separate repeatability study covered 120 samples (dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 1-7, dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 7-12, dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 12-16).
- **Optimizer:** Dragonfly, an open-source Bayesian optimization package using a Gaussian-process surrogate with Thompson sampling, expected improvement, top-two EI, and upper-confidence-bound acquisition functions, plus interspersed random exploration (dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 7-12).
- **Speedup:** ~6× time acceleration compared with random search on the same robot; ~3× workflow efficiency versus an 8 h/day human researcher; 42 experiments versus a nominally 1,000-candidate exhaustive grid represents ~96% fewer samples (dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 1-7, dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 12-16).

---

### 2. CMU Autonomous Electrochemical Test Stand — Aqueous (Whitacre et al., 2019)

This is the aqueous-electrolyte precursor to Clio, developed at Carnegie Mellon University and designed for machine-learning-informed electrolyte optimization (whitacre2019anautonomouselectrochemical pages 1-1, whitacre2019anautonomouselectrochemical pages 1-3).

- **DOI:** 10.1149/2.0521916jes (J. Electrochem. Soc., 2019); aqueous benchmarking: 10.1149/2.0142001jes (Dave et al., 2020)
- **What was dosed:** Liquids only — up to 10 solvated-salt stocks or pure solvents; aqueous LiNO₃, NaNO₃, Li₂SO₄, Na₂SO₄, and DI water; 7 mL binary blends in 1 mL increments (whitacre2019anautonomouselectrochemical pages 3-5, whitacre2019anautonomouselectrochemical pages 1-3).
- **Conductivity measurement:** Flow-through Topac K = 1.0 four-pole glass/Pt conductivity probe in custom PTFE housing, read by a Consort C3410 dual-channel analyzer; temperature-compensated to 20 °C; standard error ~0.5 mS/cm; separate three-electrode Pt/Pt/Ag-AgCl cell with PalmSens potentiostat for voltage-stability windows (whitacre2019anautonomouselectrochemical pages 1-3, dave2020benchmarkingconductivitypredictions pages 4-9).
- **Compositions per campaign:** Campaign table lists 75, 800, 70, 70, and 70 tests (totaling ~1,085); each test ~7 min; two-dimensional searches completed in <1 day (whitacre2019anautonomouselectrochemical pages 3-5, whitacre2019anautonomouselectrochemical pages 5-7).
- **Optimizer:** HTTP/Python API designed for integration with Dragonfly Bayesian optimization; the 2019 paper primarily demonstrated autonomous data gathering, with full ML integration described as future work (whitacre2019anautonomouselectrochemical pages 1-1, hu2025artificialintelligence‐drivendevelopment pages 14-14, whitacre2019anautonomouselectrochemical pages 3-3).
- **Speedup:** Searches that would take much longer manually were completed in <1 day; no defensible numerical speedup versus grid or OFAT was explicitly reported (whitacre2019anautonomouselectrochemical pages 5-7).

---

### 3. Helmholtz Institute Münster / Stein Robotic HTE System — Non-Aqueous, N₂ Atmosphere (Rahmanian et al., 2023)

A high-throughput experimentation system for non-aqueous battery electrolyte formulation with automated conductivity measurement via EIS (rahmanian2023conductivityexperimentsfor pages 1-2, rahmanian2023conductivityexperimentsfor pages 2-3).

- **DOI:** 10.1038/s41597-023-01936-3 (Scientific Data, 2023); related one-shot active-learning study: 10.1002/batt.202200228 (Rahmanian et al., 2022); related ML-aided optimization: 10.1039/d3ta06249j (Yan et al., 2024)
- **What was dosed:** Both liquids and solids — gravimetric dosing of EC, PC, EMC (liquids), and LiPF₆ (solid salt) into aluminium or polymer vials with automated closure, mixing, heating, and electrode immersion (rahmanian2023conductivityexperimentsfor pages 1-2, rahmanian2023conductivityexperimentsfor pages 2-3).
- **Conductivity measurement:** Automated electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) after thermal equilibration from −30 to 60 °C in 10 °C steps; 40 mV AC excitation over 20 kHz–50 Hz; MADAP software performed Arrhenius analysis (rahmanian2023conductivityexperimentsfor pages 2-3).
- **Compositions per campaign:** Up to 96 formulations in 8 hours; dataset comprises 504 formulation JSON files and 5,035 individual experiments/measurements; the Flores et al. symbolic-regression study used 3,626 individual measurements aggregated into 859 data points (rahmanian2023conductivityexperimentsfor pages 1-2, rahmanian2023conductivityexperimentsfor pages 2-3, flores2022learningthelaws pages 2-3).
- **Optimizer:** The 2023 dataset paper did not incorporate a closed-loop optimizer (MADAP is downstream analysis software). The related 2022 publication used one-shot active learning for globally optimal conductivity. The system operated in a controlled N₂ atmosphere (rahmanian2023conductivityexperimentsfor pages 2-3).
- **Speedup:** 96 formulations per 8 hours represents high throughput; no explicit grid/OFAT speedup was reported in the available evidence.

---

### 4. Self-Driving CO₂ Electrolyser — Aqueous (Deng et al., 2026)

This platform demonstrates closed-loop electrolyte optimization but with ethylene selectivity (not conductivity) as the feedback signal (deng2026selfdrivingco2electrolysera pages 19-26, deng2026selfdrivingco2electrolyser pages 19-26, deng2026selfdrivingco2electrolyserd pages 1-5).

- **DOI:** Not yet established in the available record (2026 manuscript).
- **What was dosed:** Liquids only — aqueous Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, and Cs⁺ stocks dispensed by precision syringe pumps through a passive four-way mixing junction; DI-water flushing between formulations; no powder dosing.
- **Measurement:** Inline DGS2 C₂H₄ gas sensor (not ionic conductivity); GC validation.
- **Compositions per campaign:** 45 unique compositions per current-density condition, initialized from 22 training points; three current densities studied; quaternary design space >170,000 compositions at 1% resolution (deng2026selfdrivingco2electrolysera pages 19-26, deng2026selfdrivingco2electrolyser pages 19-26).
- **Optimizer:** TuRBO (trust-region Bayesian optimization) with Gaussian-process surrogate (deng2026selfdrivingco2electrolyser pages 19-26).
- **Speedup:** Each formulation evaluated in <10 min; blended compositions improved relative C₂H₄ selectivity by 5–10% over best single-cation systems; no explicit grid/OFAT sample reduction reported.

---

### 5. Additional Related Platforms (Not Strict Conductivity-Closed-Loop)

**ODACell (Yik et al., 2023; DOI: 10.1039/D3DD00058C):** An affordable, modular robotic system for automated electrolyte formulation, coin-cell assembly, and galvanostatic cycling using Opentrons OT-2 liquid handling and Dobot robotic arms. Demonstrated with aqueous LiClO₄/DMSO model electrolytes. Measures cycling performance, not standalone ionic conductivity. No closed-loop optimizer; 83 cells assembled in six batches with ~2% capacity RSD (yik2023automatedelectrolyteformulation pages 2-4, yik2023automatedelectrolyteformulation pages 1-2, yik2023automatedelectrolyteformulation pages 4-6).

**Electrolab (Oh et al., 2023; DOI: 10.1016/j.device.2023.100103):** An open-source, modular platform for automated characterization of redox-active electrolytes. Uses an XYZ gantry robot, multiplexed microelectrode arrays, and Python/Arduino control. Demonstrated voltammetric screening (200 voltammograms in 2 hours) and solution titration, not bulk ionic conductivity. Bayesian optimization proposed for future work; glovebox-compatible version planned (oh2023theelectrolaban pages 1-3, oh2023theelectrolaban pages 9-10).

**SALSA (Zhang et al., 2026; DOI: 10.1039/D5DD00516G):** A ~US$100 modular add-on to the Clio/ElyteOS platform for automated salt solubility assessment. Uses a 3D-printed Archimedes-screw solid doser and computer-vision dissolution detection. Demonstrated with NaFSI in ACN, DME, and EMC. Measures solubility, not conductivity (zhang2026salsaalowcost pages 1-2, zhang2026salsaalowcost pages 2-3).

**Auto-MISCHBARES (Rahmanian et al., 2024; DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-rb9j7):** An autonomous millimetre-scale battery research system using a Hamilton Microlab 600 syringe and HELAO active-learning software. Full details were not obtainable, and ionic-conductivity measurement was not established in the available evidence (soni2025accelerateddevelopmentof pages 15-18).

**PNNL Robotic Solubility Platform (Noh et al., 2024; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-47070-5):** A closed-loop platform for discovering electrolyte solvents for non-aqueous redox-flow batteries. Dosed both solid redox-active molecules and organic solvents; measured solubility by quantitative NMR, not conductivity. Used Bayesian optimization with GP regression; screened <10% of >2,000 candidates, achieving >90% sample reduction and >13× throughput advantage (noh2024anintegratedhighthroughput pages 2-3, noh2024anintegratedhighthroughput pages 1-2).

---

### Key Observations

1. **True closed-loop conductivity optimization** has been demonstrated by very few platforms. The clearest example is **Clio/Dragonfly** (Dave et al., 2022), which is the only platform in the retrieved literature that combines automated liquid dosing, in-line ionic conductivity measurement, and Bayesian-optimization-driven next-experiment selection in a single closed loop for battery electrolyte formulation (dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 1-7).

2. **Aqueous vs. non-aqueous distinction:** The CMU Autonomous Test Stand (Whitacre et al., 2019) operated with aqueous electrolytes at ambient conditions (whitacre2019anautonomouselectrochemical pages 1-1, whitacre2019anautonomouselectrochemical pages 1-3). Clio (Dave et al., 2022) operated with non-aqueous carbonate electrolytes inside a dry-argon glovebox (dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 16-21). The Helmholtz HTE system operated under N₂ atmosphere with non-aqueous carbonates (rahmanian2023conductivityexperimentsfor pages 2-3).

3. **Platforms named in the query but not matching the specific scope:** A-Lab is a solid-state inorganic synthesis robot (not liquid electrolyte formulation); ChemOS is orchestration software used by MEDUSA for metal-ligand complexes (not electrolyte conductivity); Otto Chemistry is an organic synthesis robot; none of these were found to have demonstrated liquid electrolyte formulation with conductivity-closed-loop optimization in the retrieved literature (soni2025accelerateddevelopmentof pages 15-18).

4. **Chemspeed-based electrolyte platforms:** Although the Helmholtz/Münster group's system handles both liquid and solid dosing under inert atmosphere—capabilities consistent with Chemspeed hardware—the retrieved papers do not explicitly identify the robot manufacturer. The associated Krishnamoorthy et al. (2022; DOI: 10.1002/cmtd.202200008) data-driven analysis of high-throughput conductivity experiments was referenced but the full paper was not obtainable.

5. **Sample-count reductions:** The most quantitative claim is from Clio/Dragonfly: ~96% fewer samples versus exhaustive grid search and ~6× time acceleration versus random search (dave2022autonomousoptimizationof pages 1-7). The PNNL solubility platform (Noh et al., 2024) reported >90% sample reduction for solubility screening (noh2024anintegratedhighthroughput pages 1-2).

(2024), [10.1038/s41467-024-47070-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-47070-5) | **Non-aqueous redox-flow electrolyte; closed-loop formulation, but solubility rather than conductivity was optimized** | No glovebox requirement established; samples equilibrated for 8 hours at fixed temperature | **Powder and liquids:** robot dispensed solid 2,1,3-benzothiadiazole and 22 organic solvents; neat solvents and binary mixtures at nine volume fractions | **Not measured:** saturated samples were transferred automatically to NMR tubes and analyzed by qNMR for molar solubility | Candidate space had **22 neat solvents plus 2,079 binary formulations**; reported run produced 42 measurements in about 27 hours; overall strategy measured under 10% of a greater-than-2,000-candidate library | Bayesian optimization and active learning with a **Gaussian-process-regression surrogate** and uncertainty-aware acquisition | **Under 10% of candidates measured**, giving greater than 90% sample reduction versus exhaustive screening; about 39 min per sample and a reported greater-than-13× throughput advantage in the study comparison (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000029) |


*Table: Comparison of strict conductivity-feedback self-driving laboratories and closely related electrolyte-automation systems. It distinguishes genuine closed-loop ionic-conductivity demonstrations from platforms optimizing solubility, cycling performance, or product selectivity.*

info.query: State of the art: which self-driving laboratories / autonomous experimentation platforms have been demonstrated for LIQUID ELECTROLYTE FORMULATION, where an automated liquid-dosing system mixes multi-component solutions and IONIC CONDUCTIVITY is measured in a closed loop to select the next composition? Name the specific platforms (e.g. Clio/Dragonfly, Otto Chemistry, AMANDA/Autonomous Energy Materials Discovery, ChemOS, Chemspeed-based electrolyte platforms, A-Lab, Argonne/NREL electrolyte robots) with DOIs and publication years. For each: what was dosed (liquid only, or powders/salts too), how conductivity was measured (dip probe, flow cell, four-electrode, impedance/potentiostat), how many compositions per campaign, what optimizer was used, and what the reported speedup or sample-count reduction versus grid/one-factor-at-a-time was. Distinguish clearly between aqueous and non-aqueous (glovebox) systems.
